Write the continued fraction as θ=[a0​;a1​,a2​,…] and define its convergents by
p−1​=1,p0​=a0​,pn​=an​pn−1​+pn−2​,
(1)
q−1​=0,q0​=1,qn​=an​qn−1​+qn−2​.
(2)
Induction using these recurrences gives
pn​qn−1​−pn−1​qn​=−(pn−1​qn−2​−pn−2​qn−1​)=(−1)n−1​.
(3)
In particular, consecutive convergents have coprime numerator and denominator. The standard best-approximation consequence of the same determinant identity is that, for 0<q≤qn​ and p/q=pn​/qn​,
∣qθ−p∣>∣qn​θ−pn​∣.
(4)
Dividing by q≤qn​ gives
​θ−qp​​=q∣qθ−p∣​>qn​∣qn​θ−pn​∣​=​θ−qn​pn​​​.
(5)
The contrapositive proves that any strictly better approximation has q>qn​.
For 12​, the continued-fraction algorithm gives
12​=3+(12​−3),12​−31​=2+12​+31​,
(6)
and the remainder then repeats. Hence
12​=[3;2,6​]​.
(7)
The convergent [3;2]=7/2 supplies a solution of the Pell equation:
x=7,y=2​,72−12⋅22=1.
(8)

2H (Topics in Analysis)

Words: 219 Articles: 1
Paper 2 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 219
2H OurBigBook.com
The Legendre polynomial pn​ is orthogonal on [−1,1] to every polynomial of degree below n. Suppose it changes sign at only r<n distinct interior points x1​,…,xr​, and put
q(x)=∏j=1r​(x−xj​),
(9)
choosing its overall sign so that pn​q≥0 on [−1,1]. This product is positive except at finitely many points, so
∫−11​pn​(x)q(x)dx>0,
(10)
contradicting orthogonality because degq=r<n. Thus pn​ has at least n sign-changing roots in (−1,1); its degree is n, so these are all its roots and they are distinct.
For arbitrary distinct nodes x1​,…,xn​, let
Li​(t)=∏j=i​xi​−xj​t−xj​​
(11)
be the Lagrange basis polynomials. Every polynomial P of degree below n satisfies P(t)=∑i​P(xi​)Li​(t), so the required weights exist and are
Ai​=∫−11​Li​(t)dt.
(12)
They are unique because applying any such formula to P=Li​ recovers Ai​.
Now assume exactness for every P of degree below 2n and define Q(t)=∏i​(t−xi​). For every polynomial R of degree below n, the product QR has degree below 2n and vanishes at every node. Therefore
∫−11​Q(t)R(t)dt=0.
(13)
There is a unique monic polynomial of degree n orthogonal to all lower-degree polynomials, so Q is the monic normalization of pn​ and the xi​ are precisely the roots of pn​. Taking P=1 gives
i=1∑n​Ai​=2​.
(14)
Finally Li2​ has degree 2n−2, so exactness gives
Ai​=∑j​Aj​Li​(xj​)2=∫−11​Li​(t)2dt>0.
(15)
These are the positive weights of Gaussian quadrature.

For a discrete memoryless channel with input X and output Y, its information capacity is
C=maxpX​​I(X;Y),
(16)
where I(X;Y) is the mutual information and the maximum is over all input distributions. Capacity is measured in bits when logarithms have base two.

With rows indexed by outputs A,B,⋆ and columns by inputs A,B, the channel matrix is
​1/201/2​01/21/2​​​.
(17)
This is a binary erasure channel with erasure probability 1/2. Conditional on no erasure, the input is recovered exactly, whereas an erasure supplies no information. Thus
I(X;Y)=21​H(X),
(18)
which is maximized by the uniform input distribution. Therefore
C=21​ bit​.
(19)

Let q=P(X=B). The merged channel is a Binary Z-channel: its second output occurs with probability q/2, while the output has one bit of uncertainty only when X=B. In terms of the binary entropy function h2​,
I(X;Y)=h2​(q/2)−q.
(20)
At an interior maximum,
0=dqdI​=21​log2​q/21−q/2​−1,
(21)
so (2−q)/q=4 and q=2/5. Consequently
C=h2​(1/5)−52​=log2​45​ bits​.
(22)

Solution

Words: 108
i OurBigBook.com
A subset E⊆N is recursive when its indicator function is a total computable function. It is recursively enumerable when it is the domain of a partial computable function, equivalently when an algorithm can enumerate its members.
If E is recursive, its indicator decides both E and its complement, so both sets are recursively enumerable. Conversely, suppose programs enumerate E and N∖E. On input n, run the two enumerations in parallel by dovetailing. Exactly one must eventually print n; accept in the first case and reject in the second. This algorithm always halts and decides E. Hence
E is recursive⟺E and N∖E are recursively enumerable​.
(23)

ii

Words: 77 Articles: 1
4F OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 77
ii OurBigBook.com
The set
K={n:fn,1​(n) halts}
(24)
is the diagonal halting set. It is recursively enumerable by simulating the coded machine, but it is not recursive by the halting problem diagonal argument.
By contrast, K100​ is recursive: decode n, reject it if it is not a program code, otherwise simulate the program on input n for exactly 100 steps and accept precisely if it has halted. This bounded computation always terminates. Thus
K is not recursive,K100​ is recursive​.
(25)

b OurBigBook.com
Two packs contain 40 cigarettes. Holding height fixed, increasing average consumption from zero to two packs per day changes the log odds by
40(0.02313)=0.9252.
(27)
The corresponding odds ratio is therefore
e0.9252≈2.52​.
(28)
Thus the model estimates that a two-pack-per-day smoker has about 2.52 times the odds of heart disease of an otherwise comparable nonsmoker. This is an association in the fitted observational model, rather than by itself a causal conclusion.

Zi​=−4.50161+0.02521heighti​+0.02313cigsi​+εi​.

P(Yi​=1)=F(−4.50161+0.02521heighti​+0.02313cigsi​),
(30)
which is precisely the fitted logistic regression.

If r is measured in the rotating frame, its inertial velocity is r˙+ω×r. The masses producing the gravitational field are stationary in this frame, so their potential energy is a time-independent function V(r). Thus kinetic minus potential energy gives the stated Lagrangian
L=2m​(r˙+ω×r)2−V(r).
(42)
Put v=r˙+ω×r. Then
∂r˙∂L​=mv,∂r∂L​=−mω×v−∇V.
(43)
Substitution in the Euler-Lagrange equation yields
m(r¨+2ω×r˙+ω˙×r+ω×(ω×r))=−∇V​.
(44)
The extra terms are the Coriolis acceleration, Euler acceleration, and centrifugal acceleration of a rotating reference frame.
The canonical momentum and Hamiltonian are
p=m(r˙+ω×r)​,
(45)
H(r,p,t)=2mp2​−ω(t)⋅(r×p)+V(r)​.
(46)
Accordingly, Hamilton's equations are
r˙=mp​−ω×r,p˙​=−ω×p−∇V​.
(47)

CX∣βzx​⟩=2​∣0⟩+(−1)z∣1⟩​⊗∣x⟩=H∣z⟩⊗∣x⟩.

The required identity is
(ZzXx⊗I)∣β00​⟩=∣βzx​⟩​;
(59)
the first exponent in the scanned statement should be z. Indeed, Xx changes the parity label from 0 to x, while Zz multiplies the component whose first qubit is 1 by (−1)z, creating the phase label. Equivalently, the hint permits either one-qubit operator to be transferred to the second half of the Bell state by transposition.

This is superdense coding. To send the two classical bits (z,x), Alice applies ZzXx to her half of the shared Bell state ∣β00​⟩, producing ∣βzx​⟩, and sends that one qubit to Bob. Bob applies CX followed by H on the first qubit, as in part (i), and measures both qubits in the computational basis. The outcome is zx with certainty, so one transmitted qubit communicates two classical bits using the previously shared quantum entanglement.

11H OurBigBook.com
Label the edges so that barycentric coordinates on T satisfy
I={u=0},J={v=0},K={w=0},u+v+w=1.
(60)
Suppose for contradiction that A∩B∩C=∅. The distance from a point to a closed set gives continuous nonnegative functions dA​,dB​,dC​. Their sum never vanishes, while at every point at least one of them vanishes because A∪B∪C=T. Hence
F(x)=dA​(x)+dB​(x)+dC​(x)(dA​(x),dB​(x),dC​(x))​
(61)
is a continuous map from T to its boundary in barycentric-coordinate space. Moreover, F(I)⊆I, F(J)⊆J, and F(K)⊆K. On each edge, the straight-line homotopy between F and the identity remains in that edge, so F∣∂T​ has winding number one. On the other hand, a map from the whole triangle to its boundary makes its boundary restriction null-homotopic, and hence gives winding number zero. This contradiction proves the three-set covering lemma:
A∩B∩C=∅​.
(62)
If a retraction f:D→∂D fixed every boundary point, choose a homeomorphism from T to D taking its three edges to three consecutive closed arcs of ∂D with empty triple intersection. The inverse images under f of those arcs would be closed, would cover D, and would contain the corresponding boundary arcs. Transporting them to T would contradict the result just proved. Therefore
there is no retraction D→∂D​.
(63)
For the final statement, use compactness of the three closed arcs inside the corresponding open sets. A finite open cover of a compact metric space admits a closed shrinking, and the shrinking can be chosen to preserve specified compact subsets already lying in the respective open sets. Thus there are closed sets
A⊂P,B⊂Q,C⊂R
(64)
which cover D and contain α,β,γ, respectively. The disc version of the three-set covering lemma, obtained from the triangle by a homeomorphism taking its edges to the three arcs, gives a point in A∩B∩C. Since these sets lie in the original open sets,
P∩Q∩R=∅​.
(65)

The columns of the parity-check matrix of the binary Hamming code are precisely the n=2d−1 distinct nonzero vectors of F2d​. If h1​=h2​, then h1​+h2​ is nonzero and differs from both summands, so it occurs as a unique third column h3​.
A word supported on three positions is a codeword exactly when the corresponding three columns sum to zero. Every unordered pair of columns determines one such triple, and each triple is counted once by each of its three pairs. Therefore
ν(3)=31​(2n​)=6n(n−1)​​.
(66)

Words: 41
ii OurBigBook.com
Sum all nonzero vectors of F2d​. In each coordinate, exactly 2d−1 vectors have entry one, which is even because d>1. The sum is therefore zero, so
H1T=0.
(67)
Thus the all-one word belongs to the Hamming code and has Hamming weight n.

iii

Adding the all-one codeword is a bijection from C to itself, and it replaces every bit by its complement. It therefore sends weight j to weight n−j, proving
ν(n−j)=ν(j).
(68)
The code has one word of weight zero and, since its minimum Hamming distance is three, no words of weight one or two. Combining this with part (i) gives
ν(n−1)=0,ν(n−2)=0,ν(n−3)=6n(n−1)​​.
(69)

For nonadjacent vertices a,b, the local connectivity κ(a,b;G) is the minimum cardinality of an a-b vertex separator: a set S⊆V(G)∖{a,b} such that a and b lie in different components of G−S.
To prove the vertex form of the Menger theorem, replace every vertex v∈/{a,b} by an arc vin​→vout​ of capacity one. Replace every undirected edge uv by directed arcs from uout​ to vin​ and conversely, each of capacity larger than ∣V(G)∣; leave a,b unsplit. An integral a-b flow of value k decomposes into k paths, and the unit-capacity vertex arcs force the corresponding graph paths to be internally vertex-disjoint paths. Conversely, k such paths give an integral flow of value k.
Because a and b are nonadjacent, any finite minimum cut consists entirely of unit-capacity vertex arcs. These arcs correspond exactly to an a-b vertex separator of the same size. The max-flow min-cut theorem, whose augmenting-path proof also guarantees an integral maximum flow for integral capacities, therefore gives
max{number of internally vertex-disjoint a-b paths}=κ(a,b;G).
(106)
In particular, G contains the required set of κ(a,b;G) paths.

A 3-connected graph contains a cycle, and any cycle is a complete graph subdivision TK3​.
For TK4​, choose a cycle C for which some C-bridge has at least three attachment vertices a,b,c; such a choice is always possible in a 3-connected graph. Indeed, every component outside a cycle has at least three attachments, since one or two would form a vertex cut, and if a chosen cycle is spanning, a chord can be used to choose a smaller cycle and expose the remaining bridge. In a minimal connected part of that bridge joining a,b,c, suppress degree-two vertices. The result has a branch vertex w joined to a,b,c by three paths whose interiors are mutually disjoint and avoid C. The three arcs of C between a,b,c, together with these three paths, form a subdivision of the complete graph on branch vertices w,a,b,c. Hence
G contains a TK4​​.
(107)
A 3-connected graph need not contain a TK5​. The complete graph K4​ itself is 3-connected and has only four vertices, so it cannot contain a graph subdivision of K5​. Equally, any planar 3-connected graph is a counterexample because a subdivision of the complete graph K5​ would be nonplanar.

B(xn​,rn​)⊂B(xn−1​,rn−1​)∩Gn​,0<rn​<2−n,

Choose a countable sequence qj​↑p with 1≤qj​<p. Since ℓq⊂ℓr for q<r, every ℓq with q<p lies in some ℓqj​. For integers m≥1, set
Ej,m​={x∈ℓp:∥x∥qj​​≤m}.
(154)
Pointwise convergence and Fatou lemma for series show that Ej,m​ is closed in ℓp. It has empty interior: inside any ℓp ball, add a sufficiently long finite block whose ℓp norm is tiny but whose ℓqj​ norm is larger than m. Therefore every Ej,m​ is nowhere dense. Since ℓp is a Banach space, Baire gives
ℓp=⋃j,m​Ej,m​=⋃1≤q<p​ℓq.
(155)
An explicit element of the difference is

Write qi​=−gii​ for the total rate of leaving i. The jump chain of a continuous-time Markov chain X is the discrete-time chain Y=(Yn​) recording the states occupied after successive jumps. Its transition probabilities are
pij​=qi​gij​​(j=i),pii​=0,
(195)
whenever qi​>0.
The chain X is irreducible if every state can be reached from every other state with positive probability. A state i is recurrent if, after leaving i, the process returns to i with probability one; an irreducible chain is recurrent when one, and hence every, state is recurrent.
The continuous-time Markov chain and its jump chain have exactly the same successive states. If Y is transient, it visits each state only finitely often, so X is transient. If Y is recurrent, it visits a fixed state i infinitely often. At those visits, X has independent exponential holding times of rate qi​<∞. Their sum diverges almost surely, so explosion cannot occur before all those returns. Hence X returns to i infinitely often and is recurrent. Thus, for an irreducible chain,
X is recurrent⟺Y is recurrent.​
(196)

The Bendixson-Dulac criterion says the following. Let D⊆R2 be a simply connected domain, let F=(f,g) be continuously differentiable, and suppose there is a continuously differentiable function B such that
∇⋅(BF)=∂x∂(Bf)​+∂y∂(Bg)​
(242)
has one sign throughout D and does not vanish identically on any open subset. Then z˙=F(z) has no periodic orbit contained in D.
Indeed, if a periodic orbit Γ existed, simple connectivity would put its interior U inside D. The vector field F, and hence BF, is tangent to Γ, so its outward flux is zero. The divergence theorem would give
0=∫Γ​BF⋅nds=∬U​∇⋅(BF)dxdy,
(243)
contradicting the sign hypothesis.
The Poincaré-Bendixson theorem states that a nonempty compact omega-limit set of a continuously differentiable planar flow that contains no equilibrium point is a periodic orbit. More generally, when the omega-limit set contains only finitely many equilibria, it is either an equilibrium, a periodic orbit, or a union of equilibria and connecting trajectories.

cos(akH)sin(bkH)+absin(akH)cos(bkH)=0.
(358)
Therefore the rigid elastic waveguide mode dispersion relation is
atan(akH)=−btan(bkH)​,a=cP2​c2​−1​,b=cS2​c2​−1​​.
(359)
As c increases, both akH and bkH increase without bound. The two sides consequently have infinitely many alternating tangent branches and poles. On successive continuity intervals their relative ordering reverses, so the intermediate value theorem gives infinitely many intersections, corresponding to infinitely many propagating waveguide modes.

The mth Krylov subspace is
Km​(A,v)=span{v,Av,…,Am−1v}​.
(360)
Because A has a complete eigenbasis, decompose
v=v1​+⋯+vs​,
(361)
where vj​ is the projection of v onto the eigenspace belonging to the jth distinct eigenvalue λj​; some vj​ may vanish. Then
Akv=∑j=1s​λjk​vj​.
(362)
Every generator of Km​(A,v) therefore belongs to span{v1​,…,vs​}, and
dimKm​(A,v)≤sfor every m​.
(363)

b OurBigBook.com
For an iterate xm​, the Conjugate gradient method residual is
rm​=b−Axm​​.
(364)
Two fundamental properties are the Conjugate-gradient residual orthogonality conditions
rm​⊥Km​(A,r0​),rm​∈Km+1​(A,r0​).
(365)
Equivalently, the residuals generated before convergence are mutually orthogonal and span the successive Krylov spaces.
Since A has only s distinct eigenvalues, its minimal polynomial has degree at most s. Consequently
Ks+1​(A,r0​)=Ks​(A,r0​).
(366)
The two properties then put rs​ both inside and orthogonal to Ks​(A,r0​), so rs​=0. Hence Axs​=b, and
CG terminates after at most s iterations​.
(367)

Let e1​=(1,0,…,0)T. The displayed lower-bidiagonal matrix Q satisfies
A=QQT+e1​e1T​.
(368)
Since P=Q−1, the Preconditioned conjugate gradient method uses
PAPT=I+(Pe1​)(Pe1​)T.
(369)
Solving Qz=e1​ gives
z=Pe1​=(1,−1,1,−1,…)T,zTz=n.
(370)
The rank-one matrix I+zzT has eigenvalue 1+n in the direction z and eigenvalue 1 on the (n−1)-dimensional orthogonal complement of z. It therefore has only two distinct eigenvalues. Part (b) gives
the preconditioned method terminates after at most two iterations​.
(371)

Solution

Words: 74
d OurBigBook.com
Because A is a positive-definite matrix, it has a positive-definite inverse square root. Choose the exact inverse-square-root preconditioner
P=A−1/2​.
(372)
Then
PAPT=A−1/2AA−1/2=I,
(373)
which has one distinct eigenvalue, so preconditioned CG terminates in one step.
This construction is of little computational use because obtaining and applying A−1/2 is generally at least as expensive in storage and arithmetic as directly factoring or solving the original system. A useful preconditioner must only approximate this transformation while remaining cheap to construct and apply.
